title: Ops and risk framework for self-hosted inference
content:
Executive summary:

Quick take: engineering teams evaluating vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM stacks often underestimate operational complexity and long-tail risk (security, upgrades, cost variance). This note frames a concise ops-and-risk checklist for buyers and proposes messaging that highlights Redwood's value across three buyer personas (startup product-engineering, platform team at mid-market, regulated enterprise).

Goal: give sales and product marketing a short, repeatable set of claims, counter-arguments, and a decision checklist to move a build-vs-buy conversation toward Redwood (hosted/dedicated/private) without relying on heavy cost spreadsheets in early-stage discovery.

Context and scope:
- Focus: inference serving stacks commonly assembled from open-source components: vLLM (KV/prefix caching + scheduler), TGI (server + adapters), TensorRT-LLM (optimized kernels), plus orchestration layers (Kubernetes, KServe, custom autoscalers).
- We compare practical failure modes and buyer priorities (latency SLO, cost predictability, compliance, maintenance burden).

Key tradeoffs (short):
- Performance vs predictability: Raw latency on a bench can favor TensorRT-LLM or vLLM with careful kernel tuning; predictability under mixed workloads favors Redwood Dedicated or Private because of capacity planning, autoscaling policies, and runtime fallbacks.
- Upgrades vs stability: OSS stacks require manual model runtime updates, CVE patching, and tuning after each model change. Redwood centralizes versioning and automated rollouts.
- Unit economics vs fixed cost risk: Self-hosted can be cheaper at 24/7 high utilization but comes with overprovision/degradation risk; Redwood offers reserved capacity for predictable unit costs and hosted for variable workloads.

Ops & risk checklist (for platform evaluators):
1) Day 0: provisioning & HW fit
   - Do you have validated GPU images for every model variant (FP16/INT8 + kv-cache tuning)?
   - Do you have repeatable infra-as-code for burst pools and fallback regions?
2) Day 1: deployment & rollout
   - Canary tooling for model binary changes and tokenizer updates?
   - Automated rollback when latency or error rates cross thresholds?
3) Day 2: running ops
   - Tracing and token-level latency breakdowns (model time vs I/O vs queueing)?
   - Prefetching / prefix cache invalidation policies?
4) Security & compliance
   - KMS integrations, tenant network isolation, audit trail retention windows?
5) People & cost
   - Staff needed to tune kernels, maintain quantization scripts, and respond to performance regressions?
   - Budget for periodic refreshes (driver updates, CUDA, Triton, TRT-LLM changes)?

Concrete failure modes we've observed in PoCs:
- KV cache thrash: workload with many short, unique prompts causes cache misses, causing 3-5x token latency spikes unless engineered batching/pinning is in place.
- Model incompatibility on upgrade: Tokenizer/model mismatches during a rollout that bypassed end-to-end evaluation.
- Undetected memory leaks in custom adapters leading to OOM after hours of operation.

Short technical comparisons (notes for SEs):
- vLLM: great for flexible scheduling and prefix caching; operationally sensitive to request distribution; high reward when you can invest in runtime tuning.
- TGI (Text Generation Inference): solid adapter ecosystem and broad model compatibility; less opinionated about batching strategies; easier for teams that want near-drop-in server behavior.
- TensorRT-LLM / TRT integrations: best raw per-token throughput for supported architectures; heavy lift for maintaining optimized kernels across model updates and CPU/GPU driver changes.

Buyer personas and tailored messaging:
1) Startup product-engineering (low headcount, rapid experiments)
   - Pain: want fastest time to iterate, don’t want to hire infra experts.
   - Message: "Ship model-driven features now — Redwood hosted gets you shipping with predictable latency and no infra overhead. If needs grow, move to Dedicated with seamless config parity."
   - Objection handler: "We can run vLLM ourselves cheaper" -> "Short-term you might, but we see teams pay 2–4x in engineers + ops to keep parity when usage hits production patterns. We provide a migration path and cost/latency telemetry so you can decide later."
2) Platform team (mid-market, multi-team tenants)
   - Pain: standardize inference across teams, enforce cost controls and SLAs.
   - Message: "Unified runtime + policy routing — same API, private or dedicated infra, with role-based access + route-level cost controls."
   - Objection handler: "We have kubernetes + TRT pipelines" -> "We integrate with your ecosystem, but replace the monitoring, rollout, and billing plumbing — reducing mean time to resolution and staff load."
3) Regulated enterprise
   - Pain: compliance, auditability, private networking, long-term support.
   - Message: "Private deployment with KMS/HSM and audit retention options, backed by SLA and on-prem packaging for air-gapped needs."
   - Objection handler: "We need full control over models" -> "Private control plane gives you the control and visibility while offloading runtime continuity and security hardening to Redwood. We support model pinning and on-prem images."

Decision matrix (short, for discovery calls):
Ask two axis questions: 1) Is the workload predictable 24/7 or bursty? 2) Do you require compliance primitives (kms/audit/airgap)?
- If predictable 24/7 + low compliance: consider Dedicated or self-host (if they have ops).
- If bursty + low compliance: hosted API usually lowest TTV and ops.
- If any compliance or hard SLAs: Redwood Private or on-prem with professional services.

Cost heuristics (back-of-envelope to use in calls):
- Self-hosted arithmetic pitfalls: most teams only model GPU hour cost. They forget human recurring cost (0.25–0.5 FTE per 24/7 serving fleet per 100k qps workload), and unexpected margin from tail latencies.
- Redwood differentiated offering: hosted for low commit, dedicated for stable high QPS (saves by pooling), private for compliance—with clear add-ons (retention, support).

Recommended GTM plays and assets to create:
- One-pager "Ops-risk checklist for serving" (customer-facing checklist for platform buyers).
- Short interactive calculator that includes engineer FTE estimates, not only infra cost.
- Demo playbook: two labs — (A) migrate a TGI endpoint to Redwood Hosted in 30 minutes, (B) convert a TRT-LLM tuned model into a Dedicated pool and show failover to a cheaper model variant.
- Battlecard: objection scripts for "we'll run it ourselves" and "we need full control".

Messaging dos/don'ts (quick):
- Do: quantify predictable outcomes (SLOs, latency percentiles, cost per 1k tokens) and show concrete rollback story.
- Don't: get lost in kernel-level superiority claims unless buyer is an infra expert — instead surface who will maintain that expertise and at what ongoing cost.

Open questions & next steps:
- Build the interactive FTE-aware cost calculator (owner: go-to-market + finance).
- Create engineering playbook for the two demos and get SRE sign-off (owner: eng-platform).
- Draft a one-page customer checklist and add to the onboarding kit for AE/SEs (owner: enablement).

Notes to self: keep this doc lightweight, share with SE team before next week’s demo rehearsal.

End.
